extracted.subtask_description: Summarize newsroom policies and professional expectations about altering photographs (especially colour changes), how editors check for manipulation, and the possible professional consequences for over-manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper image manipulation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Most US papers have strict self-imposed rules forbidding photographers from manipulating images. Adjustments are allowed only when they do not significantly change the photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy distinguishes benign adjustments (that don't significantly change the photograph) from manipulations that alter the scene; the page emphasizes a strong prohibition on manipulation in US newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustments are allowed only when they do not significantly change the photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No detailed list of permitted edits is given on the page; the practical test implied is whether the edit 'significantly change[s]' the original image (e.g., colour balance changes that alter perceived scene are likely disallowed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors verify authenticity by comparing raw files
rubrics_metrics.description: A comparison between the raw file and the finished version was made [in the reported case], leading to disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may inspect raw files against submitted/printed versions to detect alterations; use on high-visibility placements (e.g., front page) increases scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for over-manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-manipulation can result in suspension, revocation of awards, firing, and published apologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the reported case of Patrick Schneider: his altered image (background changed from brownish gray to vivid orange) was used on the front page, then comparison with the raw file led to his dismissal and a later apology; he had previously been suspended and had an award revoked for similar issues.
